prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a district court abuses its discretion in denying a 28 U.S.C. 1404(a) transfer where the transferee venue is clearly more convenient.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fifth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### The District Court Abused Its Discretion in Denying Transfer Because the Transferee Venue Is Clearly More Convenient.

Section 1404(a) provides that "[f]or the convenience of parties and witnesses, in the interest of justice, a district court may transfer any civil action to any other district or division where it might have been brought." 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). The statute's purpose is "to prevent the waste of time, energy and money and to protect litigants, witnesses and the public against unnecessary inconvenience and expense." *In re Volkswagen AG*, 371 F.3d 201, 203 (5th Cir. 2004) (quotation omitted). A district court has broad discretion over transfer. But that discretion has limits. A court abuses it when it denies transfer even though the movant has shown that the transferee forum is "clearly more convenient." *In re Volkswagen of Am., Inc.*, 545 F.3d 304, 315 (5th Cir. 2008) (en banc).

**A. The governing standard.** The movant must show good cause. *Id.* To do so, the movant must "clearly demonstrate[] that a transfer is '[f]or the convenience of parties and witnesses, in the interest of justice.'" *Id.* The inquiry begins with whether the case could have been brought in the transferee venue. It then turns to the private- and public-interest factors. *Id.* The private factors are "(1) the relative ease of access to sources of proof; (2) the availability of compulsory process to secure the attendance of witnesses; (3) the cost of attendance for willing witnesses; and (4) all other practical problems that make trial of a case easy, expeditious and inexpensive." *Id.* The public factors are administrative difficulties from court congestion, the local interest in resolving local disputes, the forum's familiarity with governing law, and the avoidance of conflict-of-law problems. *Id.*

Good cause does not require the movant to show that the transferee venue is perfect. It requires only that the transferee venue be clearly more convenient. *Id.* Where it is, the statute calls for transfer. A plaintiff's choice of forum is not a separate factor. It is simply the burden the movant must meet. *Id.* at 314–15 & n.10. The choice "should be respected" only if the movant fails to show good cause. *Id.* at 315. *See also In re Horseshoe Entm't*, 337 F.3d 429, 432–33 (5th Cir. 2003) (applying the standard and treating the plaintiff's choice as a burden on the movant, not a presumption in the plaintiff's favor).

**B. A district court abuses its discretion when it ignores the factors or misweighs them.** The Fifth Circuit has repeatedly found abuse of discretion where a district court gave controlling weight to the plaintiff's choice of forum or to marginal connections to the chosen forum. It has also found abuse where the court discounted the location of witnesses and evidence. *See Volkswagen of Am.*, 545 F.3d at 315–18 (granting mandamus where the court gave too much weight to the plaintiff's choice and to tenuous local connections). *Volkswagen AG*, 371 F.3d at 203–05 (same, where the court failed to apply the 100-mile rule to witness inconvenience). The Court has also granted mandamus where a district court's reasoning does not hold up against the record. *See In re Radmax, Ltd.*, 720 F.3d 285, 287–90 (5th Cir. 2013). It has done the same where the court treated a few litigation contacts in the chosen forum as outweighing the transferee forum's connection to the dispute. *See In re Rolls Royce Corp.*, 775 F.3d 671, 675–80 (5th Cir. 2014).

The same standard of review governs on direct appeal. A denial of transfer is reviewed for abuse of discretion. A court abuses its discretion when its ruling rests on an erroneous view of the law or a clearly erroneous assessment of the evidence. *Weber v. PACT XPP Techs., AG*, 811 F.3d 758, 766 (5th Cir. 2016).

**C. Applied here, every factor points to the transferee venue.** [Insert record facts. They should show that the relevant witnesses, documents, and physical evidence are located in the transferee district. They should also show that the key non-party witnesses are beyond the compulsory process of the chosen forum but within that of the transferee court, that the events giving rise to the claim occurred in the transferee district, and that the chosen forum has no meaningful connection to the dispute.] Where, as here, the sources of proof and the witnesses are concentrated in the transferee district, the first three private factors favor transfer. The local-interest factor favors transfer as well, because the community that has a stake in the dispute is the one where the events occurred. *See Volkswagen of Am.*, 545 F.3d at 317–18. The remaining factors are neutral. Neutral factors cannot offset a clear imbalance on the others. *See Radmax*, 720 F.3d at 288–90.

The district court identified no countervailing consideration that carries real weight. Its denial of transfer therefore rested on the deference to the plaintiff's choice of forum that *Volkswagen* rejected. Its denial also reflected a misapplication of the factors that govern transfer. Both are abuses of discretion. This Court should reverse and direct transfer to the transferee venue.
